title: Mono
summary: A budgeting app that made people feel smart, not scolded — brand, product marketing, and a site that converts.
description: Mono asked for a brand that could make a budgeting app feel like a power tool instead of a guilt trip — and a marketing site sharp enough to carry it. We rebuilt both from the typography up.
imageAlt: The Mono brand system — wordmark, type specimens, and app screens on a cream board
content:
Budgeting apps all make the same promise and the same mistake: they talk to you like a disappointed parent. Mono's founders wanted the opposite — a tool that treats a budget like an instrument you play, not a diet you fail.

The problem

The product was genuinely different: local-first, no bank logins sold to anyone, one honest price. But the old site said none of that. It looked like every other fintech landing page — soft gradients, floating phones, borrowed trust. Conversion sat under one percent and nobody could explain what made Mono worth paying for in one sentence.

We started with that sentence. Three workshops later the whole brand hung off five words: your money, none of ours.

What we made

  • A wordmark cut from a modified grotesque — heavy, boxy, unmistakably not-a-bank.
  • A type-first design system: ink on cream, hard rules, one loud green reserved for numbers going the right way.
  • A marketing site rebuilt around the pricing page — the page people actually decide on — with a live, playable demo of the budget board.
Chronicle gave us a brand that sounds like us on our best day. The site finally says the thing we could never fit in a tagline.Dana Okafor — Cofounder, Mono

What happened

Trial signups tripled in the first six weeks. More telling: support stopped getting the question so what does Mono actually do? The sentence was doing its job.

title: Fieldnotes
summary: Product design for a note-taking app built for field researchers — offline-first, glove-friendly, and genuinely fast.
description: Fieldnotes is a note-taking app for people standing in a bog at 6am — biologists, surveyors, archaeologists. We designed an interface that works offline, one-handed, in gloves, and still looks good back at the desk.
imageAlt: Fieldnotes app screens — capture view and specimen log on a tablet
content:
Most productivity software is designed for someone at a desk with two free hands and a strong opinion about keyboard shortcuts. Fieldnotes' users are standing in a river. The brief was simple to say and hard to do: make capture instant, make sync invisible, make nothing precious.

Designing for wet thumbs

We threw out the standard component sizes on day one. Every tap target in capture mode is at least 56 pixels, every primary action lives in the bottom third of the screen, and the entire capture flow works with the phone upside down in a chest pocket — voice notes get transcribed and filed against the last GPS fix.

The visual language is deliberately blunt: high-contrast ink on paper tones, one accent, thick rules between records. It reads in direct sunlight and it doesn't pretend a specimen log is a lifestyle product.

The system underneath

  • A 40-component UI kit with a strict two-token color budget per screen.
  • Offline states designed first, not retrofitted — every screen has a no-signal truth.
  • A print stylesheet, because field teams still hand reports to people who like paper.
Every designer we'd worked with tried to make us look like a startup. Chronicle made us look like a tool.Dr. Imani Cole — Founder, Fieldnotes Labs

Fieldnotes shipped to beta with three national survey teams; the capture flow tested at under four seconds from pocket to filed note — half the target.

title: Koto Coffee
summary: An e-commerce build for a specialty roaster — a shop that tastes like the coffee: small, exact, and a little intense.
description: Koto roasts twelve coffees a year and sells out of most of them. They needed a shop that treats each lot like an edition drop, not a grocery shelf — and a checkout that doesn't fight the customer.
imageAlt: The Koto Coffee shop — a coffee lot page with tasting notes and a bold buy module
content:
Specialty coffee sites usually go one of two ways: minimalist to the point of mute, or so busy with origin trivia you can't find the buy button. Koto wanted a third way — treat every roast like a record release. Numbered, dated, gone when it's gone.

Lots, not products

We rebuilt the catalog around the lot: each coffee gets an edition number, a roast date, a counter of bags remaining, and a tasting card typeset like a spec sheet. Scarcity isn't a growth hack here — it's just true, and the design finally says it.

The buy module stays pinned as you read, with grind and quantity handled in two taps. Checkout is a single page. Nothing asks you to create an account; the coffee doesn't care.

Details that carried it

  • A live "bags left" counter that pulls from inventory — honest urgency.
  • Tasting notes set in a fixed grid so regulars can compare lots at a glance.
  • Packaging labels generated from the same data as the site — one source of truth from roaster to doorstep.
The site finally feels like standing at our bar. People buy in one visit now — they used to lurk for a week.Jun Sato — Owner, Koto Coffee

Average time-to-purchase dropped from six days to two, and the last four lots sold out before the following roast day.

title: Parallel
summary: Marketing site and dashboard design for a team-scheduling SaaS — the boring category, done loud.
services: Web design · Dashboard UI · Design system
description: Scheduling software is a sea of soft blue sameness. Parallel hired Chronicle to make theirs impossible to mistake for anyone else's — from the marketing page down to the empty states.
imageAlt: The Parallel dashboard — a week board with bold ink dividers and pink conflict flags
content:
Every scheduling product demos well and looks identical. Parallel's founders had a sharper wedge: conflicts. Their engine catches double-bookings and crunch weeks before they happen. So we built the whole visual identity around the moment of collision.

Make the conflict the hero

The signature element is the flag — a hard pink marker that cuts across the week board wherever two commitments collide. It's on the landing page, in the product, on the T-shirts. Where competitors soften their UI to feel calm, Parallel points at the problem and says: there.

The rest of the interface earns that loudness by being ruthlessly quiet — ink rules, generous whitespace, one type family, no decoration that isn't information.

Shipping the system

  • A shared token set between marketing site and app, so the demo is the product.
  • Empty states written like a good coworker — specific, brief, occasionally funny.
  • A component library the in-house team now extends without us, which was the point.
We stopped looking like a feature and started looking like a company.Robin Reyes — CEO, Parallel

Six months post-launch, Parallel's demo-to-trial rate had doubled, and the pink flag had become shorthand in their sales calls: nobody asks what the product does anymore.

title: Archive.fm
summary: Art direction for an online radio archive — 40 years of pirate broadcasts, catalogued like they matter. Because they do.
services: Art direction · Web design · Type system
description: A volunteer foundation digitising four decades of pirate and community radio asked for a home that felt like the medium — urgent, homemade, alive — without turning the collection into a nostalgia gift shop.
imageAlt: Archive.fm — a broadcast index page with cassette-label typography and a wall of show cards
content:
Pirate radio was never polite. The flyers were photocopied, the frequencies drifted, and the design — when there was design — was whatever the marker pen allowed. The archive holding its history shouldn't feel like a museum vitrine. It should feel like the signal got a domain name.

The visual language

We built the direction on three rules: type does the talking, every broadcast is a card you could imagine taped to a wall, and the accent color changes with the decade you're browsing. The grid is rigid; everything on it is slightly unruly — rotated labels, hand-set index numbers, timestamps in tape-deck mono.

Structure for 11,000 hours

  • A broadcast card system that scales from a single show to a full station retrospective.
  • Decade-keyed index pages, browsable like crate-digging rather than searching a database.
  • A contributor kit so volunteers can catalogue new tapes without breaking the language.
It looks like the flyers we never kept. Volunteers cried. Twice.Mika Torres — Director, Archive.fm Foundation

The archive relaunched with 11,000 catalogued hours and tripled its volunteer applications in the first quarter — apparently the design made the work look like something worth joining.

title: Tandem
summary: A full identity for a cycling apparel brand that refuses to whisper — wordmark, kit graphics, and a launch site.
description: Tandem makes cycling kit for people who ride in the city, in the rain, in traffic. The brand needed to work at 30 kph from 30 metres — high-visibility as an aesthetic, not an apology.
imageAlt: The Tandem identity — jersey graphics, wordmark lockups, and spoke-card ephemera
content:
Cycling brands split into two camps: euro-heritage serif nostalgia, or tech-bro aero minimalism. Tandem rides to work. Their kit gets rained on, locked up, and worn into meetings. The identity had to survive all three.

Legible at speed

The wordmark is built from a single ultra-wide cut — five letters that read from across an intersection. Kit graphics use blocks of the pink against ink panels, placed where drivers actually look: shoulders, back pockets, ankle cuffs. High-visibility stopped being a compliance feature and became the whole point of view.

The system in the wild

  • Three lockups — full, stacked, and a spoke-card badge — all readable in motion.
  • A pattern language cut from chevrons and lane markings, never decoration for its own sake.
  • A launch site that sells the philosophy first and the jersey second, with a fit guide written by actual commuters.
People stop us at lights to ask about the kit. That's the marketing budget now.Rae Lindqvist — Founder, Tandem

The first production run sold out in nine days, and the spoke-card badge — meant as ephemera — became the brand's most requested sticker. Loud works.
